species_ids <- 1:10

  species_id   = 1:10,
  species_code = paste0("Species_", 1:10),
  common_name  = c(
    "Ulmus carpinifolia",
    "Acer",
    "Salix aurita",

if (!dir.exists(base_dir)) {
  stop("base_dir not found — check your path!")
} else {
  total_files <- length(list.files(base_dir, pattern = "\\.tif$"))
  cat("Folder found! Total .tif files:", total_files, "\n")
}

get_species_files <- function(sp_num, base_dir, n = 10) {
  pattern <- paste0("^l", sp_num, "nr.*\\.tif$")
  files   <- list.files(base_dir,
                        pattern     = pattern,
                        full.names  = TRUE,
                        ignore.case = TRUE)
  head(files, n)
}
```

# Introduction

Accurate identification of tree species plays a critical role in
botany, ecology, and forestry, allowing scientists to monitor
biodiversity, support conservation efforts, and better understand
ecological systems. Leaf identification has long depended
on manual morphological assessment — a process that is both
time-consuming and requires considerable botanical expertise. With
computer vision and image analysis techniques continuously advancing,
automated leaf classification using measurable visual features has
become a powerful and reproducible alternative to manual
identification.

\indent The Swedish Leaf Dataset, compiled by Söderkvist (2001) at the
Computer Vision Laboratory at Linköping University, provides an ideal case
study for image-based species characterization. This project addresses the
following question: to what degree do shape and color features extracted from
scanned leaf images capture consistent within-species visual identity across
Swedish tree species, and what do patterns of within-species consistency and
between-species distance reveal about the reliability of image-based leaf
characterization?

\indent Söderkvist (2001) categorizes leaf features into four main groups:
shape and outline, inner structure, color, and surface features, identifying
shape as the most stable and reliable characteristic for species
classification. Building on this foundation, Zheng and Wang (2010) propose
a gray-scale morphology approach for extracting leaf vein patterns — the
inner structural features that shape analysis alone cannot capture. Together,
these two works provide the theoretical basis for the feature extraction
pipeline used in this report, which combines outline-based shape features
with RGB and HSV color features to build a precisely characterize each species.

This report analyzes 10 distinct species using 10 images per species,
yielding a total of 100 images. Shape features extracted from leaf
outlines cover geometric properties such as size, elongation, margin
complexity, and symmetry — how consistent these features are across
images of the same species directly reflects how reliable outline-based
identification can be. Color features from the RGB and HSV color
systems describe the chromatic properties of the leaf surface after
the background has been removed, and the standard deviations within
each species reveal how uniformly a species expresses its color across
different images. Together, these features let us determine which
species are most reliably characterized, which features best
distinguish species from one another, and where the visual boundaries
between species hold up and where they break down.

# Dataset Overview

\indent The Swedish Leaf Dataset was compiled by Söderkvist (2001)
at the Computer Vision Laboratory at Linköping University and is
publicly available at the CVL research datasets page. The dataset
contains 1,125 high-resolution scanned leaf images across 15 Swedish
tree species with 75 images per species, stored as .tif files. Images
follow a systematic naming convention — for example l9nr003.tif
refers to the third image of species 9 — making automated file
loading straightforward to implement. All leaves were scanned against
a bright white background under consistent lighting conditions,
ensuring that observed differences between species reflect genuine
morphological variation rather than imaging artifacts.

\indent For this report, 10 species are analyzed — Species 1 through
10 in the dataset — using 10 images per species, yielding a total of
100 images. These 10 species were selected to cover a range of leaf
forms while keeping processing time manageable, and the 10 images per
species provide sufficient within-species variation to compute
reliable summary statistics. Table 1 lists all 10 species included
in the analysis.

\indent Two key references guide the analytical approach. Söderkvist
(2001) establishes that leaf shape is the most stable and
discriminating feature, noting that color and surface features are
less reliable due to their sensitivity to season, lighting, and leaf
age. Zheng and Wang (2010) demonstrate that vein patterns extracted
through gray-scale morphological operations provide additional inner
structural information that shape analysis alone cannot capture.
While this report does not implement vein extraction, their pipeline
directly informs the preprocessing approach used here, particularly
the grayscale conversion and binary thresholding steps used to
isolate the leaf from the background.

```{r step1, include=FALSE}
plot_color <- function(img, main = "") {
  plot.new()
  rasterImage(as.raster(img), 0, 0, 1, 1)
  title(main = main)
}

plot_gray <- function(mat, main = "") {
  image(1:ncol(mat), 1:nrow(mat),
        t(mat[nrow(mat):1, ]),
        col  = gray(seq(0, 1, length.out = 256)),
        axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main)
}

plot_binary <- function(mat, main = "") {
  image(1:ncol(mat), 1:nrow(mat),
        t(mat[nrow(mat):1, ]),
        col  = c("black", "white"),
        axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main)
}

process_leaf_image <- function(file, threshold = 200) {
  img        <- image_read(file)
  img        <- image_resize(img, "1200x1200>")
  gray_img   <- image_convert(img, colorspace = "gray")
  gray_array <- image_data(gray_img, channels = "gray")
  gray_mat   <- matrix(as.integer(gray_array[1, , ]),
                       nrow = dim(gray_array)[2],
                       ncol = dim(gray_array)[3])
  binary_mat    <- ifelse(gray_mat > threshold, 1, 0)
  leaf_mask     <- gray_mat <= threshold
  lab           <- bwlabel(Image(leaf_mask))
  tab           <- table(as.vector(lab))
  tab           <- tab[names(tab) != "0"]
  largest_label <- as.numeric(names(tab)[which.max(tab)])
  leaf_clean    <- lab == largest_label
  leaf_clean    <- fillHull(leaf_clean)
  edge          <- leaf_clean & !erode(leaf_clean,
                                       makeBrush(3, shape = "box"))
  edge_mat      <- as.matrix(edge) * 1
  list(img        = img,
       gray_mat   = gray_mat,
       binary_mat = binary_mat,
       leaf_clean = leaf_clean,
       edge_mat   = edge_mat)
}
```

# Data Preprocessing

\indent Prior to extracting shape and color features, each leaf image
in the Swedish Leaf Dataset requires a preprocessing pipeline to
isolate the leaf from the background. Raw images are high-resolution
.tif scans captured against a bright white background, which makes
automated segmentation straightforward and consistent across all
species. The pipeline follows four stages — grayscale conversion,
binary thresholding, connected component filtering, and contour
extraction — consistent with the approach described by Söderkvist
(2001) and informed by the gray-scale morphology techniques of Zheng
and Wang (2010).

\indent Figure 1 displays the four-stage pipeline applied to a
representative leaf image from Ulmus carpinifolia. In the first
stage, the original color image is converted to grayscale, reducing
each pixel to a single brightness value between 0 and 255, which
simplifies the image while preserving the contrast between the
darker leaf tissue and the bright background. In the second stage,
a binary threshold of 200 is applied — pixels with grayscale values
greater than 200 are classified as background and set to white,
while pixels at or below 200 are classified as leaf and set to
black. In the third stage, the largest connected component is
retained using bwlabel() to remove small dark artifacts outside
the leaf, and fillHull() fills any internal holes to produce a
clean solid leaf mask. In the fourth stage, the leaf contour is
extracted using an 8-neighborhood erosion approach, where boundary
pixels are identified as leaf pixels that have at least one
background pixel among their eight immediate neighbors.

```{r pipeline-example, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Figure 1. Four-stage preprocessing pipeline applied to Ulmus carpinifolia. From left to right: original color image, grayscale image, binary image (threshold = 200), and extracted leaf contour."}
test_file <- get_species_files(1, base_dir, n = 1)
result    <- process_leaf_image(test_file, threshold)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
plot_color(result$img,        "Stage 1: Original Color Image")
plot_gray(result$gray_mat,    "Stage 2: Grayscale Image")
plot_binary(result$binary_mat,
            paste0("Stage 3: Binary (Threshold = ", threshold, ")"))
plot_binary(result$edge_mat,  "Stage 4: Leaf Contour")
```

\indent The threshold value of 200 was selected based on the imaging
characteristics of the Swedish Leaf Dataset. Figure 2 compares three
threshold values — 150, 200, and 230 — applied to the same leaf
image to justify this selection. A threshold of 150 incorrectly
excludes lighter leaf regions near the margins, producing an
incomplete leaf mask that underrepresents the true leaf area. A
threshold of 230 begins incorporating bright background pixels into
the leaf region, introducing noise along the edges that contaminates
the extracted contour. A threshold of 200 most cleanly separates
the leaf from the background, and is therefore applied consistently
across all 10 species throughout the analysis.

```{r threshold-comparison, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Figure 2. Comparison of three binary threshold values applied to the same leaf image. A threshold of 200 most cleanly separates the leaf from the background."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
for (th in c(150, 200, 230)) {
  binary_mat <- ifelse(result$gray_mat > th, 1, 0)
  plot_binary(binary_mat, paste0("Threshold = ", th))
}
```

\indent The pipeline was applied to all 10 species analyzed in this
report, confirming successful leaf isolation despite considerable
variation in leaf size, shape, and color across species. The
resulting leaf images and extracted contours for all 10 species are
presented in Figure 8 in the Species Characterization section, where
the visual profiles provide direct confirmation of the quantitative
characterizations produced by the shape and color analyses.

```{r step2, include=FALSE}
compute_perimeter4 <- function(mask) {
  mask   <- as.matrix(mask) > 0
  padded <- matrix(FALSE, nrow(mask) + 2, ncol(mask) + 2)
  padded[2:(nrow(mask)+1), 2:(ncol(mask)+1)] <- mask
  center <- padded[2:(nrow(mask)+1), 2:(ncol(mask)+1)]
  up     <- padded[1:nrow(mask),     2:(ncol(mask)+1)]
  down   <- padded[3:(nrow(mask)+2), 2:(ncol(mask)+1)]
  left   <- padded[2:(nrow(mask)+1), 1:ncol(mask)]
  right  <- padded[2:(nrow(mask)+1), 3:(ncol(mask)+2)]
  sum(center & !up) + sum(center & !down) +
    sum(center & !left) + sum(center & !right)
}

compute_perimeter8 <- function(mask) {
  mask   <- as.matrix(mask) > 0
  padded <- matrix(FALSE, nrow(mask) + 2, ncol(mask) + 2)
  padded[2:(nrow(mask)+1), 2:(ncol(mask)+1)] <- mask
  center <- padded[2:(nrow(mask)+1), 2:(ncol(mask)+1)]
  up     <- padded[1:nrow(mask),     2:(ncol(mask)+1)]
  down   <- padded[3:(nrow(mask)+2), 2:(ncol(mask)+1)]
  left   <- padded[2:(nrow(mask)+1), 1:ncol(mask)]
  right  <- padded[2:(nrow(mask)+1), 3:(ncol(mask)+2)]
  ul     <- padded[1:nrow(mask),     1:ncol(mask)]
  ur     <- padded[1:nrow(mask),     3:(ncol(mask)+2)]
  dl     <- padded[3:(nrow(mask)+2), 1:ncol(mask)]
  dr     <- padded[3:(nrow(mask)+2), 3:(ncol(mask)+2)]
  straight <- sum(center & !up)  + sum(center & !down) +
              sum(center & !left) + sum(center & !right)
  diagonal <- sum(center & !ul)  + sum(center & !ur) +
              sum(center & !dl)  + sum(center & !dr)
  straight + diagonal * sqrt(2)
}

compute_length_width <- function(mask) {
  mask   <- as.matrix(mask) > 0
  coords <- which(mask, arr.ind = TRUE)
  if (nrow(coords) < 2) return(list(length = NA, width = NA))
  pca    <- prcomp(coords, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
  scores <- pca$x
  list(length = diff(range(scores[, 1])),
       width  = diff(range(scores[, 2])))
}

compute_symmetry <- function(mask) {
  mask  <- as.matrix(mask) > 0
  cols  <- which(colSums(mask) > 0)
  mid   <- round(mean(range(cols)))
  left_area  <- sum(mask[, cols[cols <= mid]])
  right_area <- sum(mask[, cols[cols >  mid]])
  total      <- left_area + right_area
  list(left_pct  = left_area  / total * 100,
       right_pct = right_area / total * 100)
}

extract_shape_features <- function(file, sp_num, threshold = 200) {
  r    <- process_leaf_image(file, threshold)
  mask <- as.matrix(r$leaf_clean) > 0
  area    <- sum(mask)
  perim4  <- compute_perimeter4(mask)
  perim8  <- compute_perimeter8(mask)
  lw      <- compute_length_width(mask)
  compact <- (perim4^2) / (4 * pi * area)
  sym     <- compute_symmetry(mask)
  data.frame(
    species      = paste0("Species_", sp_num),
    filename     = basename(file),
    area_px      = area,
    perimeter4   = perim4,
    perimeter8   = round(perim8, 1),
    length_px    = round(lw$length, 1),
    width_px     = round(lw$width,  1),
    aspect_ratio = round(lw$length / lw$width, 3),
    compactness  = round(compact, 3),
    left_pct     = round(sym$left_pct,  1),
    right_pct    = round(sym$right_pct, 1)
  )
}

all_shape <- list()

for (sp in species_ids) {
  files <- get_species_files(sp, base_dir, n_images)
  message("Processing shape for species ", sp, "...")
  for (f in files) {
    row <- tryCatch(
      extract_shape_features(f, sp, threshold),
      error = function(e) {
        message("Skipped: ", basename(f))
        NULL
      }
    )
    if (!is.null(row)) all_shape[[length(all_shape)+1]] <- row
  }
}

shape_df <- do.call(rbind, all_shape)

shape_df$species <- species_names$common_name[
  match(shape_df$species, species_names$species_code)
]

shape_summary <- aggregate(
  cbind(area_px, perimeter4, perimeter8,
        length_px, width_px, aspect_ratio,
        compactness, left_pct, right_pct) ~ species,
  data = shape_df,
  FUN  = mean
)
shape_summary$species <- species_names$common_name
shape_summary[, -1]   <- round(shape_summary[, -1], 2)
```

# Shape Analysis

## Shape Feature Definitions

\indent Shape features are extracted from the binary leaf mask
produced by the preprocessing pipeline, with seven features computed
for each image: area, perimeter, length, width, aspect ratio,
compactness, and symmetry. Area measures the total number of pixels
belonging to the leaf, directly reflecting overall leaf size. 
Perimeter is computed using both 4-neighborhood and 8-neighborhood
connectivity — the 4-neighborhood perimeter counts boundary pixels
along the four cardinal directions, while the 8-neighborhood
perimeter incorporates diagonal neighbors weighted by $\sqrt{2}$,
producing a smoother and more geometrically accurate boundary length
estimate. Length and width are derived from principal component
analysis applied to the leaf pixel coordinates, where length
corresponds to the spread along the first principal component —
the main axis of the leaf — and width corresponds to the spread
along the second principal component. Aspect ratio divides length
by width, producing a unitless measure of elongation where values
close to 1 indicate a round or broad leaf and higher values
indicate a narrow elongated leaf. Compactness is computed as the
perimeter squared divided by $4\pi$ times the area, equaling 1
for a perfect circle and increasing with greater margin
irregularity or serration, making it particularly useful for
distinguishing species with serrated or lobed margins from those
with smooth ones. Symmetry measures the percentage of leaf area
falling on the left side of the vertical midpoint of the bounding
box, with values near 50% indicating a symmetric leaf and values
further from 50% indicating asymmetry relative to the main vein.

## What Outlines Can Characterize

\indent Leaf outlines effectively capture geometric properties that
are stable across images of the same species and meaningfully
different between species, making them a reliable foundation for
species identification. Aspect ratio reliably distinguishes narrow
elongated leaves from broad rounded ones, as the overall shape of
a leaf is a biologically stable characteristic that does not change
with season or lighting conditions. Compactness captures the
complexity of the leaf margin — a highly serrated or lobed leaf
consistently produces a much higher compactness score than a
smooth-margined leaf regardless of imaging conditions, as confirmed
by Populus tremula's compactness score of 40.27 compared to a
range of 3.66 to 11.34 across all other species. Symmetry reveals
consistent patterns in how leaf tissue is distributed relative to
the main vein, which Söderkvist (2001) identifies as a stable
morphological characteristic that reflects genuine biological
differences between species rather than imaging variation.
Together, aspect ratio, compactness, and symmetry form the most
discriminating shape features in this analysis, collectively
capable of identifying species at the extremes of the feature
distributions with high reliability.

## What Outlines Cannot Characterize

\indent Despite their stability, outline features present important
limitations that constrain their ability to fully characterize all
10 species. Color information is entirely absent from outline
analysis — Söderkvist (2001) notes that color is inherently
unreliable due to its sensitivity to season, lighting conditions,
leaf age, and position on the tree, which limits its value as a
standalone identifier but does not eliminate its usefulness as a
complementary feature. Surface texture properties such as
glossiness and hairiness, which may help distinguish visually
similar species, are similarly invisible from the outline alone.
Most critically, inner structural features such as vein patterns
— which Zheng and Wang (2010) demonstrate can be extracted through
gray-scale morphological operations — cannot be captured from the
leaf boundary alone, representing a meaningful gap in the
characterization that outline features provide. As demonstrated
in the shape results, five species — Salix aurita, Quercus, Alnus
incana, Sorbus aucuparia, and Salix alba 'Sericea' — cluster
closely in both aspect ratio and compactness, confirming that
outline features alone are insufficient to distinguish all species
and motivating the addition of color features in the following
section.

## Shape Results

\indent Figure 3 presents the distribution of four key shape features across
the 10 species analyzed. As shown in the aspect ratio plot, Betula pubescens
stands out with a median aspect ratio of 5.39, indicating leaves that are more
than five times longer than they are wide — a level of elongation not observed
in any other species. This is further confirmed by its width of only 201.88
pixels despite a length of 1,056 pixels, reflecting a characteristically
narrow leaf form. All remaining species fall between aspect ratios of 1.27 and
2.08. Among these, Salix alba 'Sericea' (2.08) and a width of 506.82 pixels
occupies a middle ground — moderately elongated but notably narrower than
Ulmus carpinifolia, making it visually intermediate between the broadest and
most elongated species. Sorbus aucuparia (1.96) and Alnus incana (1.87) are
the next most elongated after Betula pubescens and Salix alba 'Sericea', while
Ulmus carpinifolia (1.27) and Salix aurita (1.46) are the broadest and most
rounded species in the analysis.

\indent The compactness plot reveals Populus tremula as a dramatic
outlier with a score of 40.27 — more than seven times higher than
any other species in the analysis. Populus tremula is the European
aspen, a species characterized by a distinctly toothed and
irregular leaf margin that directly accounts for its exceptionally
high compactness score, reflecting genuine biological differences
in leaf morphology rather than measurement error. This is further
confirmed by its 8-neighborhood perimeter of 37,359, nearly three
times its 4-neighborhood perimeter of 12,235, providing additional
evidence of an exceptionally irregular and complex leaf boundary
unlike any other species analyzed. All remaining species produce
compactness scores between 3.66 and 11.34, with Ulmus carpinifolia
recording the second highest score at 11.34 — suggesting a
moderately irregular margin — while the remaining eight species
cluster tightly between 3.66 and 5.66, indicating predominantly
smooth leaf margins. The area plot reveals that Ulmus glabra
produces the largest leaves on average with 407,211 pixels,
followed by Sorbus aucuparia at 391,996 and Salix aurita at
342,182, while Betula pubescens produces the smallest leaves at
112,844 pixels — consistent with its narrow elongated form
identified in the aspect ratio analysis.

\indent Table 2 reveals additional patterns in leaf dimensions and
perimeter measurements that further distinguish species beyond the
box plot comparisons. Length values are relatively consistent across
species, ranging from 855.94 pixels in Acer to 1,095.06 pixels in
Populus tremula — a difference of only 239 pixels — suggesting that
length alone provides limited discriminating power and should not
be used as a standalone identifier. Width, however, shows
considerably more variation across species, with Ulmus carpinifolia
producing the widest leaves on average at 812.35 pixels — nearly
four times wider than Betula pubescens at 201.88 pixels —
reinforcing the stark contrast in leaf form between these two
species that the aspect ratio analysis identified. The 4-neighborhood
perimeter further confirms Populus tremula's unique boundary
complexity, with a value of 12,235 compared to a range of 2,827
to 5,902 across the remaining nine species, a difference that
reflects its distinctly toothed and irregular margin rather than
simply a larger leaf size. Ulmus carpinifolia records the second
highest 4-neighborhood perimeter at 5,902 — combined with its
large width of 812.35 pixels — suggesting a particularly broad
and expansive leaf shape that, alongside its strong asymmetry,
makes it one of the more distinctive species in the shape analysis.

\indent The symmetry plot reveals considerable variation in
left-right leaf balance across species, with asymmetry emerging
as one of the most biologically meaningful shape features in the
analysis. Ulmus carpinifolia exhibits the strongest asymmetry with
89.07% of its leaf area on the left side of the main vein,
followed by Quercus at 86.80% and Acer at 76.51% — a pattern
that reflects genuine morphological characteristics rather than
measurement inconsistency. The pronounced asymmetry in Ulmus
carpinifolia is particularly meaningful from a biological
standpoint, as elm leaves are characteristically asymmetric at
the base, with the two sides of the leaf differing noticeably in
size — a trait that persists consistently across all 10 images
analyzed and confirms symmetry as a reliable identifier for this
species. Alnus incana (65.04%) falls between the asymmetric and
symmetric extremes, while Sorbus aucuparia (45.32%), Ulmus glabra
(46.78%), and Salix aurita (54.26%) are the most symmetric
species, with leaf area nearly evenly distributed on both sides
of the main vein. Notably, Ulmus glabra at 46.78% left and a
large area of 407,211 pixels presents a broad symmetric leaf
profile that contrasts strongly with Ulmus carpinifolia despite
the two species sharing the same genus — suggesting that symmetry
is a more reliable distinguishing feature between these two
related species than area or aspect ratio alone, and reinforcing
that morphological divergence can occur even within the same
taxonomic group.

\indent A critical finding from the shape analysis is the degree
of overlap between several species in the middle of the feature
distributions. Salix aurita (aspect ratio 1.46, compactness 4.83),
Quercus (1.50, 4.61), Alnus incana (1.87, 4.74), Sorbus aucuparia
(1.96, 3.66), and Salix alba 'Sericea' (2.08, 3.94) are all
closely grouped in both aspect ratio and compactness, producing
feature profiles that are nearly indistinguishable from one
another by shape alone. This overlap directly addresses the
research question — shape features reliably characterize species
at the extremes of the feature distributions, as demonstrated by
Betula pubescens (aspect ratio 5.39) and Populus tremula
(compactness 40.27), but show limited discriminating power for
species with similar overall forms, confirming that color features
are necessary to complete the characterization of these five
overlapping species.

\indent The consistency of shape features within each species
provides important evidence about the reliability of outline-based
characterization across the 10 species analyzed. Betula pubescens
shows the tightest interquartile range in aspect ratio, indicating
that its narrow elongated form is highly stable and reproducible
across all 10 images, making it the most reliably characterized
species by shape alone. Populus tremula similarly shows the
tightest range in compactness, confirming that its irregular
boundary is a stable characteristic that persists consistently
across images rather than reflecting variation in individual
leaves. In contrast, Quercus and Alnus incana show wider
interquartile ranges in both area and aspect ratio, reflecting
greater within-species variability that reduces the reliability
of these features as identifiers for these two species
specifically. Ulmus carpinifolia shows the widest range in
symmetry, suggesting that while its leaves are consistently
asymmetric, the degree of asymmetry varies noticeably across
individual images — a finding that highlights the distinction
between a feature being directionally consistent and being
precisely reproducible. Collectively, these patterns of
within-species consistency and variability directly address the
research question, confirming that the reliability of shape-based
leaf characterization depends not only on between-species
differences but on the stability of features within each species
across multiple images.

```{r shape-boxplots, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Figure 3. Distribution of four shape features across 10 species. Aspect ratio measures elongation, compactness measures margin irregularity, area measures leaf size, and symmetry measures the percentage of leaf area on the left side of the main vein."}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(10, 4, 3, 1))

boxplot(aspect_ratio ~ species, data = shape_df,
        main     = "Aspect Ratio by Species",
        xlab     = "",
        ylab     = "Aspect Ratio",
        col      = "lightblue",
        las      = 2,
        cex.axis = 0.6)

boxplot(compactness ~ species, data = shape_df,
        main     = "Compactness by Species",
        xlab     = "",
        ylab     = "Compactness",
        col      = "lightgreen",
        las      = 2,
        cex.axis = 0.6)

boxplot(area_px ~ species, data = shape_df,
        main     = "Area by Species",
        xlab     = "",
        ylab     = "Area (pixels)",
        col      = "lightyellow",
        las      = 2,
        cex.axis = 0.6)

boxplot(left_pct ~ species, data = shape_df,
        main     = "Symmetry (Left %) by Species",
        xlab     = "",
        ylab     = "Left Side %",
        col      = "lightcoral",
        las      = 2,
        cex.axis = 0.6)
```

\indent Table 2 presents the average shape features across all 10
species, providing a comprehensive numerical summary of the patterns
identified in Figure 3. The values confirm that Betula pubescens
and Populus tremula are the most uniquely identifiable species based
on shape features alone — Betula pubescens through its extreme
aspect ratio of 5.39 and Populus tremula through its extreme
compactness score of 40.27, both of which are far removed from all
other species in the analysis. The remaining eight species show
considerably greater overlap in shape characteristics, particularly
in aspect ratio and compactness, with five species — Salix aurita,
Quercus, Alnus incana, Sorbus aucuparia, and Salix alba 'Sericea'
— producing feature profiles that are nearly indistinguishable from
one another. These findings reinforce that shape features alone are
insufficient to precisely characterize all 10 species and that
color features are necessary to resolve the ambiguities that remain
among the overlapping central cluster.

```{r shape-table}
knitr::kable(shape_summary,
             caption  = "Table 2. Average shape features by species.",
             digits   = 2,
             format   = "latex",
             booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "scale_down", "hold_position"),
    full_width    = FALSE,
    font_size     = 7
  )
```

```{r step3, include=FALSE}
extract_color_features <- function(file, sp_num, threshold = 200) {
  r    <- process_leaf_image(file, threshold)
  mask <- as.matrix(r$leaf_clean) > 0
  img  <- r$img
  rgb_array <- image_data(img, channels = "rgb")
  R_mat <- matrix(as.integer(rgb_array[1,,]),
                  nrow=dim(rgb_array)[2], ncol=dim(rgb_array)[3])
  G_mat <- matrix(as.integer(rgb_array[2,,]),
                  nrow=dim(rgb_array)[2], ncol=dim(rgb_array)[3])
  B_mat <- matrix(as.integer(rgb_array[3,,]),
                  nrow=dim(rgb_array)[2], ncol=dim(rgb_array)[3])
  R_leaf <- R_mat[mask]
  G_leaf <- G_mat[mask]
  B_leaf <- B_mat[mask]
  hsv    <- rgb2hsv(r=R_leaf, g=G_leaf, b=B_leaf,
                    maxColorValue=255)
  data.frame(
    species  = paste0("Species_", sp_num),
    filename = basename(file),
    mean_R   = round(mean(R_leaf), 2),
    mean_G   = round(mean(G_leaf), 2),
    mean_B   = round(mean(B_leaf), 2),
    sd_R     = round(sd(R_leaf),   2),
    sd_G     = round(sd(G_leaf),   2),
    sd_B     = round(sd(B_leaf),   2),
    mean_H   = round(mean(hsv["h",]), 4),
    mean_S   = round(mean(hsv["s",]), 4),
    mean_V   = round(mean(hsv["v",]), 4),
    sd_H     = round(sd(hsv["h",]),   4),
    sd_S     = round(sd(hsv["s",]),   4),
    sd_V     = round(sd(hsv["v",]),   4)
  )
}

all_color <- list()

for (sp in species_ids) {
  files <- get_species_files(sp, base_dir, n_images)
  message("Processing color for species ", sp, "...")
  for (f in files) {
    row <- tryCatch(
      extract_color_features(f, sp, threshold),
      error = function(e) {
        message("Skipped: ", basename(f))
        NULL
      }
    )
    if (!is.null(row)) all_color[[length(all_color)+1]] <- row
  }
}

color_df <- do.call(rbind, all_color)

color_df$species <- species_names$common_name[
  match(color_df$species, species_names$species_code)
]

color_summary <- aggregate(
  cbind(mean_R, mean_G, mean_B, sd_R, sd_G, sd_B,
        mean_H, mean_S, mean_V, sd_H, sd_S, sd_V) ~ species,
  data = color_df,
  FUN  = mean
)
color_summary$species <- species_names$common_name
color_summary[, -1]   <- round(color_summary[, -1], 4)
```

# Color Analysis

## Why Color Features Are Needed

\indent As demonstrated in the shape analysis, shape features alone
prove insufficient to distinguish all 10 species, particularly
among the five species — Salix aurita, Quercus, Alnus incana,
Sorbus aucuparia, and Salix alba 'Sericea' — that cluster closely
in both aspect ratio and compactness, producing feature profiles
that are nearly indistinguishable from one another by outline
alone. Color features provide complementary information about leaf
physiology and condition that outline analysis cannot capture —
different species exhibit systematically different amounts of
chlorophyll, surface wax, and pigmentation, which manifest as
measurable and consistent differences in RGB and HSV color
characteristics across images of the same species. However,
Söderkvist (2001) cautions that color is not fully stable, as it
varies with season, lighting conditions, leaf age, and position
on the tree — a limitation reflected in the low coefficient of
variation for Mean Hue (8.82%) and Mean Saturation (8.91%)
identified in the feature effectiveness analysis. For this reason,
color features are analyzed alongside shape features rather than
as standalone identifiers, and within-species standard deviations
are used throughout this section to assess how consistently each
species expresses its color characteristics across the 10 images
analyzed.

## RGB Analysis

\indent The RGB color system describes each pixel using three
channels — Red, Green, and Blue — each ranging from 0 to 255,
where higher values indicate greater intensity of that color
component. Only leaf pixels are included in the color analysis,
with background pixels masked out during the preprocessing
pipeline to ensure that computed color statistics reflect the
leaf surface exclusively. Figure 4 presents the mean RGB and HSV
values averaged across 10 images per species, providing a
comprehensive overview of the color characteristics of each
species.

```{r color-plots, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Figure 4. Mean RGB channel values (top row) and mean HSV values (bottom row) by species averaged across 10 images per species. The dashed green line on the Hue plot marks the pure green reference value of 0.33."}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(10, 4, 3, 1))

barplot(color_summary$mean_R,
        names.arg = color_summary$species,
        main      = "Mean Red Channel",
        ylab      = "Mean R (0-255)",
        col       = "lightcoral",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.55)

barplot(color_summary$mean_G,
        names.arg = color_summary$species,
        main      = "Mean Green Channel",
        ylab      = "Mean G (0-255)",
        col       = "lightgreen",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.55)

barplot(color_summary$mean_B,
        names.arg = color_summary$species,
        main      = "Mean Blue Channel",
        ylab      = "Mean B (0-255)",
        col       = "lightblue",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.55)

barplot(color_summary$mean_H,
        names.arg = color_summary$species,
        main      = "Mean Hue",
        ylab      = "Hue",
        col       = "gold",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.55)
abline(h = 0.33, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)

barplot(color_summary$mean_S,
        names.arg = color_summary$species,
        main      = "Mean Saturation",
        ylab      = "Saturation",
        col       = "lightgreen",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.55)

barplot(color_summary$mean_V,
        names.arg = color_summary$species,
        main      = "Mean Brightness",
        ylab      = "Value",
        col       = "lightblue",
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.55)
```

\indent Figure 4 reveals meaningful variation in RGB channel values
across the 10 species analyzed. The Red channel ranges from 60.49
in Quercus to 86.86 in Ulmus glabra, with Ulmus glabra (86.86)
and Salix alba 'Sericea' (83.43) producing the highest Red values
and Quercus (60.49) and Betula pubescens (69.75) producing the
lowest. The Green channel follows a similar pattern — Ulmus glabra
(87.15) and Salix alba 'Sericea' (87.34) produce the highest
Green values, while Quercus (49.51) produces by far the lowest,
more than 37 points below the next lowest species Acer (66.51).
This unusually low Green value for Quercus is a particularly
notable finding — despite being a green-leafed species, its
relatively dark appearance produces lower RGB values across all
three channels compared to most other species, reflecting a
genuine difference in leaf pigmentation rather than an imaging
artifact. The Blue channel shows the most dramatic variation
across species, ranging from 6.28 in Betula pubescens to 29.88
in Sorbus aucuparia — a nearly fivefold difference that makes
the Blue channel the most discriminating RGB feature in the
analysis. Betula pubescens stands out with an exceptionally low
Blue value of 6.28 — less than half the Blue value of any other
species — indicating a very pure green color with almost no blue
component, consistent with its highest saturation value of 0.9529
identified in the HSV analysis. At the other extreme, Sorbus
aucuparia (29.88), Ulmus glabra (21.39), and Populus tremula
(20.90) record the three highest Blue values, giving these
species a slightly cooler green tone, while the remaining species
cluster between 10.13 and 18.15.

\indent The standard deviations of RGB channels provide critical
evidence about within-species color consistency across the 10
images analyzed per species. Populus tremula shows the highest
variability across all three channels with sd_R of 34.21, sd_G
of 34.95, and sd_B of 44.91 — by far the most variable species
in RGB color — a finding that is consistent with its complex and
irregular leaf boundary identified in the shape analysis and
suggests that its surface color is similarly heterogeneous across
the leaf surface. In contrast, Salix alba 'Sericea' shows the
lowest RGB variability with sd_R of 23.34, sd_G of 22.61, and
sd_B of 23.57, indicating highly consistent color expression
across images and establishing it as one of the most reliably
characterized species by color in the analysis. Ulmus glabra
similarly shows low variability with sd_R of 21.52 and sd_G of
22.13, further supporting its characterization as a species with
stable and reproducible color properties — a finding consistent
with its low Hue standard deviation of 0.0163 identified in the
HSV analysis.

## HSV Analysis

\indent The HSV color system describes each pixel using three
components — Hue, Saturation, and Value — and is particularly
useful for leaf analysis because it separates color type from
brightness, making it easier to identify meaningful differences
between species that may appear similar in overall brightness but
differ in color tone. Hue indicates the basic color type on a
scale from 0 to 1, where values near 0.33 represent pure green,
values below 0.20 represent yellow-green tones, and values above
0.33 represent blue-green tones. Saturation describes how vivid
or pure the color is, with lower values appearing more grayish,
and Value measures brightness, with higher values corresponding
to lighter leaves. Figure 4 presents mean Hue, Saturation, and
Value averaged across 10 images per species, with the dashed
green line on the Hue plot marking the pure green reference
value of 0.33.

\indent The Hue analysis reveals that all 10 species produce mean
Hue values between 0.1272 and 0.1750 — well below the pure green
reference of 0.33 — confirming that all species express a
yellow-green tone consistent with scanned leaf images. Despite
this overall similarity, meaningful differences exist between
species that carry discriminating power. Salix alba 'Sericea'
produces the highest mean Hue of 0.1750, indicating the most
green-toned leaves in the analysis, while Quercus produces the
lowest at 0.1272, followed by Sorbus aucuparia (0.1439) and Acer
(0.1500) — indicating a notably more yellow-green tone in these
three species compared to the rest. Within-species Hue standard
deviations are consistently low across most species, with Salix
alba 'Sericea' (sd_H 0.0174), Ulmus glabra (0.0163), and Salix
aurita (0.0211) showing the most stable Hue values, confirming
that color tone is a reliable and reproducible characteristic for
these species. Populus tremula, by contrast, shows the least
stable Hue with sd_H of 0.0718 — more than four times higher
than Salix alba 'Sericea' — indicating highly inconsistent color
tone across its images, consistent with the high RGB variability
identified in the prior section.

\indent Saturation values range from 0.6760 in Sorbus aucuparia
to 0.9529 in Betula pubescens, revealing considerable variation
in color vividness across species. Betula pubescens produces the
most vivid and pure green color of all species at 0.9529 —
consistent with its extremely low Blue channel value of 6.28
identified in the RGB analysis — while Salix alba 'Sericea'
(0.9147) and Quercus (0.8779) also show high saturation. Sorbus
aucuparia at 0.6760 is a clear outlier, with a saturation more
than 0.17 points below the next lowest species Ulmus glabra
(0.8014), indicating a notably muted and grayish green appearance
that distinguishes it colorimetrically from all other species
despite its otherwise average shape profile. Within-species
Saturation standard deviations further reveal important
consistency patterns — Betula pubescens shows the lowest sd_S
of 0.1442, confirming highly consistent color vividness across
images and reinforcing its status as one of the most reliably
characterized species in the analysis, while Acer shows the
highest sd_S of 0.2276, indicating considerable variability in
how vividly its color is expressed across different images and
reducing the reliability of saturation as an identifier for
this species specifically.

\indent Value — measuring leaf brightness — ranges from 0.2380
in Quercus to 0.3479 in Ulmus glabra, with Ulmus glabra (0.3479)
and Salix alba 'Sericea' (0.3456) producing the brightest leaves
and Quercus (0.2380) and Betula pubescens (0.2805) producing the
darkest. The brightness contrast between Quercus and Ulmus glabra
is particularly striking — Ulmus glabra is nearly 46% brighter
on average, a difference that is clearly visible in the bar plot
and reflects a genuine difference in leaf surface properties
between these two species. Within-species Value standard
deviations reveal that Salix alba 'Sericea' shows the lowest
sd_V of 0.0892, indicating very consistent brightness across
images and further establishing it as one of the most reliably
characterized species across all three HSV components, while
Populus tremula shows the highest sd_V of 0.1349 — reinforcing
its standing as the most color-variable species in the dataset
across Hue, Saturation, and Value simultaneously.

## HSV Distributions by Species

\indent Figure 5 presents the full HSV and RGB pixel-level
distributions for three representative species — Betula pubescens,
Quercus, and Sorbus aucuparia — selected to represent the most
vivid, darkest, and most muted color profiles in the dataset
respectively. These histograms reveal the complete shape of the
color distribution within each leaf image, providing additional
evidence about within-species color consistency that summary
statistics alone cannot capture.

\indent The Hue distributions in Figure 5 reveal important
pixel-level patterns across the three representative species.
Betula pubescens shows a consistently narrow and concentrated
Hue distribution, confirming highly uniform color tone across
the leaf surface and supporting its characterization as one of
the most reliably identified species by color. Sorbus aucuparia,
by contrast, displays a bimodal Hue distribution with a primary
peak around 0.15 and a secondary peak between 0.5 and 0.9 —
a finding not visible in the mean Hue value of 0.1439 alone —
suggesting the presence of two distinct color zones on the leaf
surface that reflect genuine within-leaf color variation rather
than imaging noise. Quercus shows a narrow Hue distribution
consistent with its low sd_H of 0.0373, confirming that despite
its unusually low mean Hue of 0.1272, its color tone is stable
and reproducible across the leaf surface.

\indent Saturation distributions are dominated by a sharp spike
near 1.0 across all three species, indicating that the vast
majority of leaf pixels are highly saturated regardless of
species. This pattern is particularly notable for Sorbus
aucuparia — despite its low mean saturation of 0.6760, its
histogram reveals that the low mean is driven by a subset of
lower-saturation pixels rather than a uniformly spread
distribution, suggesting localized color variation across the
leaf surface rather than globally muted color. Betula pubescens
shows the sharpest and most concentrated saturation spike near
1.0, consistent with its highest mean saturation of 0.9529 and
lowest sd_S of 0.1442, confirming that nearly all of its leaf
pixels express highly vivid color with minimal variation.

\indent Value distributions are approximately right-skewed across
all three species, peaking between 0.2 and 0.4 with a tail
extending toward higher brightness values. Quercus shows the
leftmost Value peak, consistent with its lowest mean brightness
of 0.2380, while Sorbus aucuparia peaks further right consistent
with its mean brightness of 0.3167. The Red channel distributions
provide additional insight — Quercus shows a broad spread from
0 to 200 peaking around 50 to 75, reflecting its wide range of
red intensities across the leaf surface, while Betula pubescens
shows a tighter Red distribution peaking around 75 consistent
with its low sd_R of 25.33. Both Betula pubescens and Quercus
show Blue channel histograms almost entirely concentrated below
25, consistent with their very low mean Blue values of 6.28 and
11.96 respectively, while Sorbus aucuparia shows a notably wider
Blue distribution extending to 50 and beyond — consistent with
its highest mean Blue value of 29.88 and directly confirming
that the Blue channel is the most discriminating RGB feature
for distinguishing Sorbus aucuparia from the other species.

```{r hsv-histograms, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Figure 5. HSV and RGB pixel distributions for three representative species — Betula pubescens (most vivid), Quercus (darkest), and Sorbus aucuparia (most muted)."}
representative_species <- c(6, 4, 10)

for (sp in representative_species) {
  sp_label <- species_names$common_name[sp]
  f        <- get_species_files(sp, base_dir, n = 1)
  r        <- process_leaf_image(f, threshold)
  mask     <- as.matrix(r$leaf_clean) > 0
  img      <- r$img

  rgb_array <- image_data(img, channels = "rgb")
  R_mat <- matrix(as.integer(rgb_array[1,,]),
                  nrow=dim(rgb_array)[2], ncol=dim(rgb_array)[3])
  G_mat <- matrix(as.integer(rgb_array[2,,]),
                  nrow=dim(rgb_array)[2], ncol=dim(rgb_array)[3])
  B_mat <- matrix(as.integer(rgb_array[3,,]),
                  nrow=dim(rgb_array)[2], ncol=dim(rgb_array)[3])

  R_leaf <- R_mat[mask]
  G_leaf <- G_mat[mask]
  B_leaf <- B_mat[mask]
  hsv    <- rgb2hsv(r=R_leaf, g=G_leaf, b=B_leaf,
                    maxColorValue=255)

  par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  hist(hsv["h",], breaks=30,
       main=paste0(sp_label, " - Hue"),
       xlab="H", col="gold")
  hist(hsv["s",], breaks=30,
       main=paste0(sp_label, " - Saturation"),
       xlab="S", col="lightgreen")
  hist(hsv["v",], breaks=30,
       main=paste0(sp_label, " - Value"),
       xlab="V", col="lightblue")
  hist(R_leaf, breaks=30,
       main=paste0(sp_label, " - Red"),
       xlab="R", col="lightcoral", xlim=c(0,255))
  hist(G_leaf, breaks=30,
       main=paste0(sp_label, " - Green"),
       xlab="G", col="lightgreen", xlim=c(0,255))
  hist(B_leaf, breaks=30,
       main=paste0(sp_label, " - Blue"),
       xlab="B", col="lightblue", xlim=c(0,255))
}
```

## Color Summary Table

\indent Table 3 presents the complete color feature summary
averaged across 10 images per species, providing a comprehensive
numerical reference for the patterns identified across the RGB
and HSV analyses. Collectively, these values confirm that color
features provide important complementary information to shape
features — particularly for the five species that overlap closely
in shape characteristics and cannot be reliably distinguished by
outline alone. Quercus and Sorbus aucuparia are especially well
differentiated by color despite their similar shape profiles —
Quercus records the lowest Hue (0.1272), lowest Green channel
(49.51), and lowest Value (0.2380) of all species analyzed,
while Sorbus aucuparia records the lowest Saturation (0.6760)
and highest Blue channel (29.88), giving each species a
distinctive color fingerprint that shape features alone cannot
capture and confirming that color analysis successfully resolves
at least part of the ambiguity left by the shape analysis.
Alnus incana presents a middle-ground color profile with mean
RGB values of 73.84, 72.96, and 12.97 and a mean Hue of 0.1617,
placing it among the most colorimetrically average species in
the dataset and making it one of the harder species to identify
by either shape or color alone — a finding that underscores the
need for additional features such as vein patterns to complete
its characterization. Ulmus carpinifolia similarly occupies a
central color position with a mean Hue of 0.1618 and moderate
saturation of 0.8851, though its high asymmetry score of 89.07%
from the shape analysis provides the primary identifying
characteristic for this species — reinforcing the central
finding of this report that the most reliable characterization
combines evidence from both shape and color features
simultaneously rather than relying on either alone.

```{r color-table}

  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "scale_down", "hold_position"),
    full_width    = FALSE,
