  )
```

```{r step4, include=FALSE}
master_summary <- merge(shape_summary, color_summary,
                        by = "species")

normalize <- function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))

feature_matrix <- data.frame(
  aspect_ratio = shape_summary$aspect_ratio,
  compactness  = shape_summary$compactness,
  area         = shape_summary$area_px,
  left_pct     = shape_summary$left_pct,
  mean_H       = color_summary$mean_H,
  mean_S       = color_summary$mean_S,
  mean_V       = color_summary$mean_V,
  mean_R       = color_summary$mean_R,
  mean_G       = color_summary$mean_G,
  mean_B       = color_summary$mean_B
)
rownames(feature_matrix) <- species_names$common_name
dist_matrix <- as.matrix(dist(scale(feature_matrix)))

char_df <- data.frame(
  Species    = species_names$common_name,
  Shape      = ifelse(shape_summary$aspect_ratio > 2.5,
                      "Narrow/Elongated", "Broad/Rounded"),
  Margin     = ifelse(shape_summary$compactness > 15,
                      "Irregular/Serrated", "Smooth"),
  Symmetry   = ifelse(abs(shape_summary$left_pct - 50) < 10,
                      "Symmetric", "Asymmetric"),
  Color_Tone = ifelse(color_summary$mean_H < 0.15,
                      "Yellow-Green",
                      ifelse(color_summary$mean_H < 0.20,
                             "Typical Green", "Blue-Green")),
  Vividness  = ifelse(color_summary$mean_S > 0.9,
                      "Very Vivid",
                      ifelse(color_summary$mean_S > 0.8,
                             "Moderately Vivid", "Muted")),
  Brightness = ifelse(color_summary$mean_V > 0.33,
                      "Bright",
                      ifelse(color_summary$mean_V > 0.27,
                             "Moderate", "Dark"))
)
```

# Species Characterization

\indent This section synthesizes the shape and color findings from
the preceding analyses to build a precise characterization of each
of the 10 species analyzed, directly addressing the research
question by assessing the degree to which combined shape and color
features capture consistent within-species visual identity and
reveal meaningful between-species boundaries. Figure 6 presents
a radar chart comparing all 10 species across seven normalized
features — aspect ratio, compactness, area, symmetry, hue,
saturation, and brightness — where each axis is scaled from 0
to 1 relative to the range of values observed across species,
allowing direct visual comparison of each species' combined
feature profile. Figure 7 presents the pairwise distance heatmap,
which quantifies the overall similarity between every pair of
species across all 10 shape and color features combined, with
darker cells indicating more similar species pairs and lighter
cells indicating more different ones. Together, these two
visualizations provide the most comprehensive view of species
separability in this analysis, revealing which species are most
reliably characterized, which pairs are hardest to distinguish,
and where the visual boundaries between species are strongest
and most fragile.

```{r radar-chart, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Figure 6. Radar chart comparing all 10 species across seven normalized shape and color features. Each axis represents one feature scaled from 0 to 1. Species further from the center on a given axis score higher on that feature relative to all others."}
normalize <- function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))

radar_data <- data.frame(
  aspect_ratio = normalize(shape_summary$aspect_ratio),
  compactness  = normalize(shape_summary$compactness),
  area         = normalize(shape_summary$area_px),
  symmetry     = normalize(shape_summary$left_pct),
  hue          = normalize(color_summary$mean_H),
  saturation   = normalize(color_summary$mean_S),
  brightness   = normalize(color_summary$mean_V)
)
rownames(radar_data) <- species_names$common_name
radar_data <- rbind(rep(1, ncol(radar_data)),
                    rep(0, ncol(radar_data)),
                    radar_data)

colors_border <- c("#E41A1C","#377EB8","#4DAF4A","#984EA3",
                   "#FF7F00","#A65628","#F781BF","#999999",
                   "#66C2A5","#FC8D62")
colors_fill <- adjustcolor(colors_border, alpha.f = 0.1)

par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
radarchart(radar_data,
           axistype   = 1,
           pcol       = colors_border,
           pfcol      = colors_fill,
           plwd       = 2,
           cglcol     = "grey",
           cglty      = 1,
           axislabcol = "grey",
           vlcex      = 0.8,
           title      = "Species Comparison — Shape & Color Features")

legend("topright",
       legend = species_names$common_name,
       col    = colors_border,
       lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       cex = 0.5, bty = "n")
```

```{r heatmap, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Figure 7. Pairwise distance heatmap across all 10 shape and color features combined. Darker cells indicate more similar species pairs and lighter cells indicate more different species pairs."}
feature_matrix <- data.frame(
  aspect_ratio = shape_summary$aspect_ratio,
  compactness  = shape_summary$compactness,
  area         = shape_summary$area_px,
  left_pct     = shape_summary$left_pct,
  mean_H       = color_summary$mean_H,
  mean_S       = color_summary$mean_S,
  mean_V       = color_summary$mean_V,
  mean_R       = color_summary$mean_R,
  mean_G       = color_summary$mean_G,
  mean_B       = color_summary$mean_B
)
rownames(feature_matrix) <- species_names$common_name

dist_matrix <- as.matrix(dist(scale(feature_matrix)))

dist_df <- data.frame(
  Species1 = rep(rownames(dist_matrix), each  = nrow(dist_matrix)),
  Species2 = rep(rownames(dist_matrix), times = nrow(dist_matrix)),
  Distance = as.vector(dist_matrix)
)

ggplot(dist_df, aes(x=Species1, y=Species2, fill=Distance)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="darkgreen", high="white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1, size=7),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size=7)) +
  labs(title    = "Pairwise Distance Between Species",
       subtitle = "Darker = more similar, Lighter = more different",
       x="", y="", fill="Distance")
```

\indent The radar chart in Figure 6 immediately highlights the two
most distinctive species in the dataset. Betula pubescens (brown)
extends dramatically outward on the aspect ratio axis — the only
species to reach near 100% on this dimension — confirming its
uniquely narrow elongated form with an aspect ratio of 5.39 that
is more than 2.5 times higher than the next most elongated
species. Simultaneously, Betula pubescens reaches near the outer
edge on the saturation axis with a mean saturation of 0.9529,
combining high elongation with vivid color to produce the most
visually distinctive overall profile in the dataset. Populus
tremula (grey) extends dramatically outward on the compactness
axis — the only species to reach near 100% on this dimension —
reflecting its compactness score of 40.27, a level of boundary
complexity that is in a category of its own relative to all
other species. These two species occupy opposite extremes of the
feature space and are the most reliably characterized species in
the entire analysis, each defined by a single dominant feature
that no other species approaches.

\indent The remaining axes of the radar chart reveal additional
patterns in species separability. The symmetry axis shows a
clear split between asymmetric and symmetric species — Ulmus
carpinifolia (red) and Quercus (purple) extend furthest,
consistent with their left side percentages of 89.07% and
86.80% respectively, while Sorbus aucuparia, Ulmus glabra, and
Betula pubescens cluster near the center reflecting their
near-symmetric profiles. The saturation axis distinguishes
Sorbus aucuparia (orange) as the species extending least far —
consistent with its uniquely low mean saturation of 0.6760 —
while Betula pubescens and Salix alba 'Sericea' extend furthest
with saturation values of 0.9529 and 0.9147 respectively. The
brightness axis shows Salix alba 'Sericea' (pink) and Ulmus
glabra (teal) extending furthest, consistent with their highest
mean brightness values of 0.3456 and 0.3479, collectively
confirming that these two species are the most reliably
characterized by brightness among all species analyzed.

\indent The pairwise distance heatmap in Figure 7 quantifies
the overall similarity between every pair of species across all
10 shape and color features combined. The darkest cell in the
heatmap — indicating the most similar pair — corresponds to
Alnus incana and Salix aurita, confirming the computed most
similar pair in the dataset. These two species share nearly
identical profiles across all features: both are broad and
rounded with aspect ratios of 1.87 and 1.46, both have smooth
margins with compactness scores of 4.74 and 4.83, both express
typical green tones with mean Hue values of 0.1617 and 0.1676,
and both show moderate saturation of 0.8744 and 0.8291 and
moderate brightness of 0.2994 and 0.3150 respectively. This
degree of similarity across both shape and color features
confirms that Alnus incana and Salix aurita are the hardest
pair to distinguish reliably using image-based characterization
alone, and that additional features such as vein patterns or
surface texture — as described by Zheng and Wang (2010) and
Söderkvist (2001) respectively — would likely be required to
separate them.

\indent At the opposite extreme, the lightest cell in the
heatmap — indicating the most different pair — corresponds to
Ulmus glabra and Quercus, confirming the computed most
different pair. Ulmus glabra and Quercus differ substantially
across multiple dimensions simultaneously: Ulmus glabra has
the largest area (407,211 pixels) while Quercus has a much
smaller area (321,667 pixels); Ulmus glabra is nearly symmetric
(46.78% left) while Quercus is strongly asymmetric (86.80%
left); Ulmus glabra has the highest brightness (0.3479) while
Quercus has the lowest (0.2380); and Ulmus glabra has a higher
Hue (0.1667) while Quercus records the lowest Hue in the
dataset (0.1272). The fact that these two species differ across
area, symmetry, brightness, and Hue simultaneously — four
independent feature dimensions — makes their combined distance
the largest in the dataset and confirms that their
characterization is the most reliable of any pair analyzed,
consistent with the research question's focus on identifying
where visual boundaries between species are strongest.

\indent The heatmap also reveals important clustering patterns
among the remaining species. Acer (aspect ratio 2.04,
compactness 3.95, Hue 0.1500, saturation 0.8206), Alnus incana,
and Salix aurita form a visibly dark cluster in the heatmap,
indicating that these three species are mutually similar and
represent the most challenging group to distinguish by combined
shape and color features. All three share broad rounded shapes,
smooth margins, typical green tones, and moderate saturation
and brightness — a convergence of similar feature values across
both shape and color that limits the reliability of
image-based characterization for this group. Salix alba
'Sericea' shows moderate distance from most other species —
darker cells with Ulmus glabra and Salix aurita but lighter
cells with Quercus and Betula pubescens — reflecting its
intermediate position in the feature space with the highest
Hue in the dataset (0.1750), a distinctive brightness of
0.3456, and high saturation of 0.9147 that partially separates
it from the central cluster. Sorbus aucuparia shows moderate
to light distances from most species, with its unique
combination of lowest saturation (0.6760) and highest Blue
channel (29.88) providing a partially distinctive color
profile that distinguishes it from the central cluster despite
an otherwise average shape.

\indent Table 4 presents a categorical summary of each species
across seven characterization dimensions derived from the
combined shape and color analysis. Betula pubescens is the
only species classified as narrow and elongated with an aspect
ratio of 5.39, making it immediately identifiable by outline
alone, while Populus tremula is the only species classified as
having an irregular or serrated margin with a compactness score
of 40.27 — together, these two species represent the clearest
cases of reliable shape-based identification in the analysis.
Among the remaining eight species, all classified as broad and
rounded with smooth margins, symmetry and color features become
the primary discriminating tools. Ulmus carpinifolia (89.07%
left) and Quercus (86.80% left) are the only strongly
asymmetric species — Quercus further distinguished by the
lowest brightness (0.2380) and lowest Hue (0.1272) in the
dataset, giving it the most distinctive combined profile among
the smooth-margined species. Salix alba 'Sericea' and Ulmus
glabra are the only two species classified as bright with
brightness values of 0.3456 and 0.3479, while Salix alba
'Sericea' further distinguishes itself with the highest Hue
(0.1750) and high saturation (0.9147). Sorbus aucuparia stands
alone as the only species with muted color vividness (saturation
0.6760), making it the most colorimetrically distinctive species
among the eight smooth-margined species despite an otherwise
average shape profile (aspect ratio 1.96, compactness 3.66) —
a finding that confirms color features successfully resolve at
least one ambiguity that shape features alone cannot.

```{r char-table}
knitr::kable(char_df,
             caption  = "Table 4. Categorical characterization summary
             of all 10 species across shape and color dimensions.",
             format   = "latex",
             booktabs = TRUE) |>
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("striped", "scale_down", "hold_position"),
    full_width    = FALSE,
    font_size     = 8
  )
```

\indent Figure 8 presents a representative leaf image and extracted
contour for each of the 10 species, providing visual confirmation
of the quantitative characterizations produced by the shape and
color analyses. The narrow elongated form of Betula pubescens —
quantified by its aspect ratio of 5.39 and width of only 201.88
pixels — is immediately visible in its contour image, producing
a distinctly thin outline that is unlike any other species in
the analysis and directly confirms its status as the most
shape-distinctive species. The irregular serrated boundary of
Populus tremula — reflected in its compactness score of 40.27
and 8-neighborhood perimeter of 37,359 — is clearly visible as
a highly complex and jagged contour that stands in stark
contrast to the smooth outlines of all other species, visually
confirming that its extreme compactness score reflects genuine
morphological complexity rather than a measurement artifact.
The strong asymmetry of Ulmus carpinifolia (89.07% left) is
clearly visible in both the leaf image and contour, with
substantially more tissue on one side of the main axis —
a visual confirmation of the symmetry analysis that identifies
this species as the most asymmetric in the dataset. The broad
symmetric profiles of Ulmus glabra (46.78% left, area 407,211
pixels), Salix aurita (54.26% left), and Sorbus aucuparia
(45.32% left) produce clean rounded contours that are visually
similar to one another, consistent with their close proximity
in the pairwise distance heatmap and reinforcing the critical
finding that these species cannot be reliably distinguished
by shape alone and require color features to complete their
characterization.

```{r species-profiles, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Figure 8. Representative leaf images (top two rows) and extracted contours (bottom two rows) for all 10 species analyzed."}
par(mfrow = c(4, 5), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))

for (sp in species_ids) {
  sp_label <- species_names$common_name[sp]
  f        <- get_species_files(sp, base_dir, n = 1)
  result   <- process_leaf_image(f, threshold)
  plot_color(result$img, sp_label)
}

for (sp in species_ids) {
  sp_label <- species_names$common_name[sp]
  f        <- get_species_files(sp, base_dir, n = 1)
  result   <- process_leaf_image(f, threshold)
  plot_binary(result$edge_mat, paste0(sp_label, " contour"))
}
```

```{r step5, include=FALSE}
cv <- function(x) sd(x) / mean(x) * 100

feature_effectiveness <- data.frame(
  Feature = c("Aspect Ratio","Compactness","Area",
              "Symmetry","Mean Hue","Mean Saturation",
              "Mean Brightness","Mean Red","Mean Green",
              "Mean Blue"),
  CV = round(c(
    cv(shape_summary$aspect_ratio),
    cv(shape_summary$compactness),
    cv(shape_summary$area_px),
    cv(shape_summary$left_pct),
    cv(color_summary$mean_H),
    cv(color_summary$mean_S),
    cv(color_summary$mean_V),
    cv(color_summary$mean_R),
    cv(color_summary$mean_G),
    cv(color_summary$mean_B)
  ), 2)
)
feature_effectiveness <- feature_effectiveness[
  order(feature_effectiveness$CV, decreasing = TRUE), ]

diag(dist_matrix) <- NA

min_idx <- which(dist_matrix == min(dist_matrix, na.rm=TRUE),
                 arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
most_similar <- paste(rownames(dist_matrix)[min_idx[1]],
                      "and",
                      colnames(dist_matrix)[min_idx[2]])

max_idx <- which(dist_matrix == max(dist_matrix, na.rm=TRUE),
                 arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
most_different <- paste(rownames(dist_matrix)[max_idx[1]],
                        "and",
                        colnames(dist_matrix)[max_idx[2]])
```

# Conclusion

\indent This report characterized 10 Swedish tree leaf species
from the Swedish Leaf Dataset using morphological shape features
extracted from leaf outlines and chromatic color features
extracted from RGB and HSV color systems, with 10 images per
species yielding a total of 100 images analyzed. The analysis
addressed the following question: to what degree do shape and
color features capture consistent within-species visual identity,
and what do patterns of within-species consistency and
between-species distance reveal about the reliability of
image-based leaf characterization? The findings demonstrate
that shape and color features together provide a reliable basis
for characterizing most species, but that their discriminating
power varies substantially across both individual features and
species pairs — a pattern that reflects genuine differences in
the morphological and chromatic distinctiveness of each species
rather than limitations of the methodology.

## Feature Effectiveness

\indent Figure 9 presents the coefficient of variation for each
of the 10 features extracted in this analysis, ranked from most
to least discriminating, to assess which features contribute
most reliably to species characterization. The coefficient of
variation measures how much a feature varies across species
relative to its mean — higher values indicate features that
differ more between species and are therefore more useful for
characterization — and provides a direct quantitative basis for
evaluating the reliability of each feature as an identifier
across the 10 species analyzed.

```{r feature-effectiveness, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Figure 9. Feature effectiveness ranked by coefficient of variation. Features with CV above 20% shown in dark green are considered highly discriminating across species."}
par(mar = c(8, 4, 3, 1))
barplot(feature_effectiveness$CV,
        names.arg = feature_effectiveness$Feature,
        main      = "Feature Effectiveness (Higher = More Useful)",
        ylab      = "Coefficient of Variation (%)",
        col       = ifelse(feature_effectiveness$CV > 20,
                           "darkgreen", "lightgreen"),
        las       = 2,
        cex.names = 0.8)
abline(h = 20, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

\indent Figure 9 reveals compactness as by far the most
discriminating feature in the analysis, with a coefficient of
variation of 130.51% — more than twice the CV of any other
feature. This extreme discriminating power is almost entirely
driven by Populus tremula's compactness score of 40.27, which
is more than seven times higher than all other species,
confirming that compactness is the single most reliable feature
for species identification when a highly irregular or serrated
leaf is present. Aspect ratio ranks second with a CV of 56.13%,
driven primarily by Betula pubescens at 5.39 — more than 2.5
times the next highest species — establishing it as the second
most discriminating shape feature and confirming that the two
most reliably characterized species in the analysis are each
defined by a single dominant shape feature. Mean Blue channel
ranks third with a CV of 42.28%, driven by the contrast between
Betula pubescens at the low extreme (6.28) and Sorbus aucuparia
at the high extreme (29.88) — a nearly fivefold difference —
making the Blue channel the most discriminating color feature
in the analysis and the only color feature to rank among the
top three overall. Area ranks fourth with a CV of 32.15%,
reflecting the substantial size variation from Betula pubescens
(112,844 pixels) to Ulmus glabra (407,211 pixels), while
symmetry ranks fifth with a CV of 27.93%, capturing the
contrast between strongly asymmetric species such as Ulmus
carpinifolia (89.07% left) and nearly symmetric species such
as Sorbus aucuparia (45.32% left).

\indent The five features above the red dashed threshold of
20% CV — compactness, aspect ratio, Mean Blue, area, and
symmetry — collectively represent the most reliable set of
features for image-based leaf characterization, with three
shape features and only one color feature among the top five
discriminators. In contrast, the five features below the
threshold — Mean Green (14.83%), Mean Brightness (10.48%),
Mean Red (9.86%), Mean Saturation (8.91%), and Mean Hue
(8.82%) — show limited between-species variation and
contribute less to species discrimination, a pattern that
is consistent with Söderkvist (2001)'s observation that color
features are less stable and reliable than shape features
across varying imaging conditions. The low CV of Mean Hue
(8.82%) is particularly notable — while all 10 species
express yellow-green tones, the differences in Hue between
species are small relative to within-species variation,
limiting its discriminating power and confirming that Hue
alone is insufficient for reliable species identification.
Mean Saturation (8.91%) similarly shows limited variation,
as most species cluster between 0.82 and 0.95 with only
Sorbus aucuparia (0.6760) as a meaningful outlier —
reinforcing that the most reliable color features for
discrimination are those tied to the extremes of the
distribution rather than the central tendency.

## Reliability of Characterization

\indent The patterns of within-species consistency and
between-species distance collectively reveal that the
reliability of image-based leaf characterization is not
uniform across species — it depends directly on the degree
to which a species expresses a distinctive and stable visual
identity across multiple feature dimensions simultaneously.
Species at the extremes of the most discriminating features
— Betula pubescens in aspect ratio (5.39) and compactness,
Populus tremula in compactness (40.27), Ulmus carpinifolia
in symmetry (89.07% left), and Quercus in Hue (0.1272) and
brightness (0.2380) — are the most reliably characterized
because their defining features are both highly consistent
within the species across 10 images and highly distinct from
all other species, producing tight interquartile ranges that
confirm stable and reproducible visual identities.

\indent In contrast, the five species in the central cluster
— Acer, Alnus incana, Salix aurita, Salix alba 'Sericea',
and Ulmus glabra — show considerable overlap in the most
discriminating features, making them harder to characterize
reliably from shape and color alone. Alnus incana and Salix
aurita represent the most extreme case of this overlap —
confirmed as the most similar pair in the dataset — with
nearly identical aspect ratios (1.87 and 1.46), compactness
scores (4.74 and 4.83), Hue values (0.1617 and 0.1676), and
saturation values (0.8744 and 0.8291) that produce feature
profiles indistinguishable from one another across both shape
and color dimensions. The reliability of characterization for
these two species is fundamentally limited by the convergence
of their visual properties, and their discrimination would
require additional features beyond shape and color — most
likely vein pattern extraction following Zheng and Wang (2010)
or surface texture analysis as described by Söderkvist (2001)
— reinforcing that the limits of image-based characterization
are not methodological but biological in nature.

\indent Ulmus glabra and Quercus represent the opposite extreme
as the most different pair in the dataset, separated by large
and simultaneous differences across area (407,211 vs 321,667
pixels), symmetry (46.78% vs 86.80% left), brightness (0.3479
vs 0.2380), and Hue (0.1667 vs 0.1272). The fact that these
two species differ across four independent feature dimensions
at once makes their combined distance the largest in the
dataset and confirms that their characterization is the most
reliable of any pair analyzed — a finding consistent with
the research question, which proposed that species expressing
distinctive visual identities across multiple feature types
simultaneously would be the most reliably characterized by
image-based methods. The contrast between Alnus incana and
Salix aurita on one end and Ulmus glabra and Quercus on the
other establishes the practical boundaries of image-based
leaf characterization — from species pairs that are nearly
indistinguishable to species pairs that are maximally
separable — and provides a clear framework for understanding
where automated leaf identification is most and least reliable.

## Limitations

\indent Several limitations arose in this analysis and should be
considered when interpreting these findings. Color features are
not fully stable across imaging conditions — as Söderkvist (2001)
notes, leaf color varies with season, lighting, leaf age, and
position on the tree — a limitation directly reflected in the low
CV values for Mean Hue (8.82%) and Mean Saturation (8.91%),
which are the two least discriminating features in the analysis
and would likely be even less reliable across images collected
under varying conditions. The binary threshold of 200 was
selected by visual inspection and may not be optimal for all
images across all species — a more principled threshold
selection method such as Otsu's method, as described by Zheng
and Wang (2010), could produce more consistent and reproducible
segmentation results and reduce the sensitivity of the pipeline
to imaging variation. Symmetry was approximated using the
vertical midpoint of the bounding box rather than the true main
vein position — a more precise symmetry measure using the vein
extraction technique of Zheng and Wang (2010) would produce
more biologically meaningful results and strengthen the
reliability of symmetry as an identifier, particularly for
species such as Ulmus carpinifolia where the degree of
asymmetry varies noticeably across images. Only 10 of 75
available images per species were used, which may not fully
capture the within-species variation present in the full
dataset — species with high within-species variability such
as Populus tremula (sd_R 34.21, sd_H 0.0718) may produce
different characterizations with a larger sample, and the
reliability of the characterizations presented here should
be interpreted with this constraint in mind. Finally, inner
structural features such as vein patterns were not extracted
in this analysis — incorporating vein analysis following Zheng
and Wang (2010) would provide an additional layer of
characterization that could resolve the ambiguities that
remain between the most similar species pairs, particularly
Alnus incana and Salix aurita, whose nearly identical shape
and color profiles suggest that vein structure may be the
most promising distinguishing feature between them.

## Conclusion

\indent Shape and color features extracted from scanned leaf
images provide a reliable basis for characterizing most Swedish
tree leaf species, with the discriminating power of individual
features varying substantially across the feature set in a
pattern that reflects genuine differences in species
morphological and chromatic distinctiveness. Compactness
(CV 130.51%), aspect ratio (CV 56.13%), and Mean Blue channel
(CV 42.28%) emerge as the three most discriminating features,
collectively capable of identifying the most visually
distinctive species — Betula pubescens, Populus tremula, and
Sorbus aucuparia — with high reliability. The pairwise distance
analysis confirms that Ulmus glabra and Quercus are the most
separable pair in the dataset while Alnus incana and Salix
aurita are the least separable, establishing clear and
quantifiable boundaries for where image-based characterization
succeeds and where it reaches its limits — a finding that
directly and precisely answers the research question posed at
the outset of this report.

\indent The biological and computational findings converge to
establish that reliable leaf characterization requires
combining multiple feature types simultaneously rather than
relying on shape or color alone. Shape features successfully
identify species with extreme geometric properties — Betula
pubescens through its narrow elongation (aspect ratio 5.39)
and Populus tremula through its irregular margin (compactness
40.27) — but fail to distinguish the five species in the
central cluster that share similar aspect ratios and
compactness scores. Color features provide complementary
information that partially resolves these ambiguities,
particularly through the Blue channel (CV 42.28%) and
saturation, but the low CV values of Hue (8.82%) and
Saturation (8.91%) confirm Söderkvist (2001)'s caution that
color is inherently less stable than shape as an identifying
characteristic and should be treated as a supplementary
rather than primary identifier. Together, the patterns of
within-species consistency and between-species distance
reveal that image-based leaf characterization is most
reliable for species that express distinctive visual
identities across multiple feature dimensions simultaneously
— as demonstrated by Betula pubescens and Populus tremula
— and least reliable for species that share similar shapes
and similar color profiles — as demonstrated by Alnus incana
and Salix aurita — a finding that motivates future work
incorporating vein pattern extraction following Zheng and
Wang (2010) and surface texture analysis following Söderkvist
(2001) to complete the characterization of the most visually
similar species in the dataset.

# References

Söderkvist, Oskar. 2001. "Computer Vision Classification of Leaves from
Swedish Trees." Master's Thesis, Linköping University. Computer Vision
Laboratory, Department of Electrical Engineering, Linköping University,
Sweden.

Zheng, Xiaodong, and Xiaojie Wang. 2010. "Leaf Vein Extraction Based on
Gray-Scale Morphology." *International Journal of Image, Graphics and
Signal Processing* 2(2): 25--31.
